entities.summary:
William Stanhope, 1st Earl of Harrington, was a British statesman and diplomat who played a pivotal role in the development of the British East India Company during the early 18th century. Born in 1679 to Thomas Stanhope, 1st Earl of Chesterfield, and his wife Catherine Wrottesley, Stanhope was educated at Eton College and later at Trinity College, Cambridge. He began his diplomatic career in 1701, serving as a secretary to the Earl of Godolphin, and later became a member of Parliament for the borough of Richmond. Stanhope's involvement with the British East India Company, which was instrumental in establishing trade routes and expanding British influence in Asia, was instrumental in shaping the company's governance and administration. He was appointed as the Governor of the East India Company's presidency in Madras in 1719, a position he held until 1723. Stanhope's tenure as governor was marked by significant reforms, including the introduction of new laws and regulations to improve the company's governance and administration. He also played a key role in the company's expansion into the Indian subcontinent, particularly in the region of Bengal. Stanhope's legacy as a statesman and diplomat has been recognized for his contributions to the development of the British East India Company and his role in shaping the company's governance and administration. He died on December 8, 1756, at the age of 77.


Stanhope's diplomatic career was also marked by his involvement in the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1713, which established trade relations between the two nations. He played a key role in negotiating the treaty, which had significant consequences for the British economy and the balance of power in Europe. Stanhope's involvement in the treaty also marked the beginning of a long-standing relationship between Britain and the Netherlands, which would have far-reaching consequences for global trade and commerce.
